And then at the end of my prompt I will say something like OK this has been a whole lot of brainstorming in different directions. So the actual session itself with Claude includes a whole lot of rambling and brainstorming, but then the actual documented artifacts of the session are the nice clean summary of what we figured out. And then, for example, when we move from a brainstorming design phase into a coding implementation phase, I'll start a brand new session so that it's context isn't polluted by the brainstorming and rambling but is rather starting off with the nicely organized document that had been created as the artifact from the previous session.

And this is why dictation works so well as a feature. What do vanguardist communism, feudalism, liberal democracy, and fascism have in common? A shared belief that the general population is composed of a bunch of dumb dumbs that need super smart (read: politically educated) people to "lead" them.

Seems subjective. When is the smartness, big smart enough to allow someone to enter the hallowed ranks of "actually a real human allowed to speak for the masses?"

There does seem to be a clear delineation between the people you hear about (the vanguard in our example), and the people you don't hear about (the masses): willingness to create confrontation. Most people want to just go with the flow, live in peace. In a dichotomy I've been calling "choose peace or violence," they choose peace. They choose to see bad things in the world or their life and focus on managing their happiness around it.

I think that this is the default human mode of existence, and that this mode lacks defenses against people willing to violate the default peace. Imagine a bagel line, and someone cutting that line, and when tapped on the shoulder, the cutter breaking into a huge tantrum, and people in line backing down with a "Jesus! It's not worth it, fine." Thus some people learn that they can be much more selfish in life if they're willing to create confrontation and disturb the peace.

When I talk to people about agitation, civil disobedience, or even just unionizing, the most common thing I hear is anxiety. What if the situation gets worse, what if there's reprisals, what if I lose this little bit of comfort that I've managed to be happy with? That slice could get smaller and smaller but people aren't willing to take the step to say "enough is enough" because I think it fundamentally goes against human nature, we have to sacrifice our own happiness on some level to put our foot down and demand or make change. At minimum we have to acknowledge the discomfort or injustice, which is a diversion from our constructed internal peace.

Personally I think people should be allowed to live in peace. Maybe the liberal democrats and vanguardist communists are right, maybe most people shouldn't need to trouble themselves with the greater direction of their society. However I think the stability this promises is false; in fact I think all stability is false. I think this constructed peace that people are afraid to disrupt clearly can be torn apart at any moment, not just by people willing to create conflict, but by a literal earthquake, or fire, or plague. Therefore I think there's a couple societies in history that got it right: ones who distributed the responsibility of society across all individuals in the society; namely the brief period of syndicalized Spain, and the several hundred thousand years of certain tribes of native Americans on the eastern portion of the continent. There may be other societies in history, these are just the cases I've been able to read about so far.

It seems to me that it's possible and necessary for all people to be ready to wake out of their constructed peace long enough to make adjustments together to maintain it. I don't think this is the same thing as them being "led out of it," I think this is each individual being on some level alert to the need to spontaneously say "no, here we wait in line for our bagels. I wrote plimsoll for my own projects. Several have an agent writing and running code, and they all needed the same things: a way for that code to call my APIs without holding a credential, a record of exactly what ran with checksums I can verify, and a way to tie each run to my own logs. I also wanted one place to use several sandboxes, local or cloud, so I can test on my machine and flip a switch for production.

Plimsoll is a Go daemon you run yourself, and the switch is its configuration: WebAssembly or plain docker on a laptop; docker under gVisor, or E2B and Docker Cloud microVMs, in production. The client code doesn't change. Every result states its isolation tier (process, container, kernel or vm), and a request can set a minimum, so code that needs a VM can't quietly run on my test setup: below the floor, nothing runs. E2B and Docker Cloud bill by the second and agents never get bored, so each caller can get a daily allowance of microVM seconds. An agent that wants to loop forever loops until the allowance runs out; the next run is refused before it starts.

Sessions keep one sandbox across calls, with Python or JavaScript cells that keep their state like a notebook (on docker, E2B and NVIDIA's OpenShell). Every response carries a run record, SHA-256 hashes of the request and result that the clients recompute; in a session the records chain, and a separate tool, plimsoll-attest, signs them and refuses a chain with a call missing. Pass your own trace ID and it lands on the daemon's audit line.

The code gets no network by default. To call one of my APIs it goes through a broker outside the sandbox: the run's grant lists the exact routes allowed, and the broker adds a token minted for that run, which never enters the sandbox, and enforces call and size budgets. It traces each call by the route pattern it matched (/items/*, not /items/42), status, size and timing, never the body or token; the audit line gets the totals, and an optional advisor flags waste, like an agent fetching 200 items one at a time, which is the most agent thing an agent can do.

To try it you only need Go (process tier, so not for hostile code):

  git clone https://github.com/plimsollmark/plimsoll && cd plimsoll
  go run ./examples/minimal
On Linux with docker, the same example at the kernel tier:

  sudo ./docker/install-gvisor.sh && make docker-images
  SANDBOX_PROVIDER=docker SANDBOX_DOCKER_RUNTIME=runsc go run ./examples/minimal
Clients: Go, Python (tools for Agno, CrewAI and Google ADK) and TypeScript (Vercel AI SDK, Trigger.dev, Mastra).

What it isn't yet: pre-1.0, no other users, no outside security audit, and it's just me: the bus factor is one, and I'm careful around buses. gVisor is Linux only, so a Mac gets the container tier. The tier is configuration plus startup smoke tests, not attestation.

If you run agent-written code today, what do you run it in? Would a tier label change what you trust?
